patient.name: Maya Ostrowski
patient.chiefComplaint: Difficulty breathing and throat tightness after a bee sting

history.hpi: Stung by a bee on the right forearm approximately 10 minutes prior to EMS arrival while gardening. Within minutes developed diffuse hives, lip and tongue swelling, and progressively hoarse voice with difficulty breathing. No known prior severe reaction to bee stings.
history.lastOralIntake: Light breakfast approximately 2 hours prior to onset
history.events: Patient was gardening when stung on the right forearm; stinger still visible. Spouse called 911 when swelling and breathing difficulty developed; no epinephrine auto-injector available in the home.

scene.location: Suburban home, back porch steps adjacent to garden
scene.safety: No hazards to crew; bee/wasp activity noted in the garden area, exercise caution
scene.bystanders: Spouse present, called 911, reports no epinephrine auto-injector available in the home
visualCues: Visible stinger embedded in right forearm with surrounding erythema and swelling
Diffuse urticaria across torso and arms
Patient sitting forward, drooling, anxious and wide-eyed

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 25-year-old female in obvious distress approximately 10 minutes after a bee sting, with audible stridor, facial/tongue angioedema, diffuse urticaria, and a muffled voice.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Audible inspiratory stridor, visible tongue and lip swelling, patient drooling and leaning forward
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic at 28/min, poor air movement, using accessory muscles
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak and thready, skin flushed
otherFindings: Diffuse urticaria across torso and arms
Visible stinger in right forearm with surrounding swelling
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "My throat... feels like it's closing..." (muffled, effortful)

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in anterolateral thigh (adult fixed dose; may repeat q5–15 min)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Epinephrine administration is the primary treatment for anaphylaxis. If signs of anaphylaxis, administer epinephrine 1 mg/mL at the following dose and route: Adult (25 kg or more) 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
expectedActions.rationale: Epinephrine is first-line therapy for anaphylaxis and must not be delayed for a patient with airway compromise.

expectedActions.shortAction: Nebulized epinephrine 5 mL (1 mg/mL) for audible stridor
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If stridor is present, consider administering epinephrine 1 mg/mL, 5 mL nebulized
expectedActions.rationale: Nebulized epinephrine directly targets upper airway edema causing the stridor.

expectedActions.shortAction: IV normal saline bolus 1,300 mL (65 kg × 20 mL/kg) rapidly over 15 min for hypoperfusion
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For signs of hypoperfusion, also administer 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid (normal saline or lactated Ringer's) rapidly (over 15 minutes) via IV or IO, and repeat as needed for ongoing hypoperfusion
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects distributive hypotension from anaphylaxis alongside epinephrine.

expectedActions.shortAction: Continuously monitor airway; stage video laryngoscopy/SGA for an anticipated difficult airway
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Anticipate, identify, and plan for a potentially difficult airway. Optimize the patient for any advanced airway attempts
expectedActions.rationale: Progressive angioedema can obstruct the airway quickly; early preparation avoids a crisis intubation.

transitions.if: IM and nebulized epi given, fluids started
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes anaphylaxis with airway compromise and hypoperfusion, administering IM epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine for stridor, and an IV fluid bolus while preparing for a potentially difficult airway.
Crew delays repeat epinephrine and advanced airway preparation; as the initial epinephrine effect wanes, laryngeal edema progresses toward near-complete obstruction.

phases.name: IM and nebulized epi given, fluids started
phases.description: Crew administers IM epinephrine and nebulized epinephrine for stridor, starts an IV fluid bolus for hypoperfusion, and prepares difficult-airway equipment in anticipation of rapidly progressing angioedema.
phases.triggerCondition: The crew recognizes anaphylaxis with airway compromise (stridor, angioedema) and hypoperfusion (hypotension, weak pulses), administering epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh, followed by nebulized epinephrine for stridor and an IV fluid bolus, while staging equipment for a potentially difficult advanced airway.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Stridor improved but still present; angioedema stable, not worsening
otherFindings: IM epinephrine administered to right anterolateral thigh
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can breathe a little better now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue cardiac/airway monitoring en route; transport promptly given biphasic-reaction risk
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport as soon as possible, and perform ongoing assessment as indicated. Cardiac monitoring is not required, but should be considered for those with known heart problems or who received multiple doses of epinephrine
expectedActions.rationale: Anaphylaxis can recur hours after apparent resolution; continued monitoring during transport catches a biphasic reaction early.

transitions.condition: With epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine, and IV fluids on board, stridor resolves, oxygenation normalizes, and perfusion improves.

phases.name: Airway remains patent, patient improves
phases.description: Stridor resolves and oxygenation normalizes following epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine, and IV fluids. Crew continues close monitoring en route given the risk of a biphasic reaction.
phases.triggerCondition: With epinephrine, nebulized epinephrine, and IV fluids on board, the patient's stridor resolves, oxygenation normalizes, and perfusion improves; the crew continues close airway monitoring en route given the risk of a biphasic reaction.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 18, clear and equal, good air movement
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel like I can breathe again."

phases.name: Airway management delayed
phases.description: As the initial epinephrine effect wanes without repeat dosing or advanced airway preparation, laryngeal edema progresses rapidly toward near-complete upper airway obstruction.
phases.triggerCondition: Despite the initial epinephrine dose, the crew delays repeat epinephrine and advanced airway preparation. As epinephrine's effect wanes, laryngeal edema progresses rapidly toward near-complete upper airway obstruction, producing severe stridor, retractions, and desaturation despite supplemental oxygen.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Severe stridor, minimal air movement, worsening tongue and lip swelling
clinicalPresentation.breathing: RR 34, marked accessory muscle use, see-saw chest movement
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact but patient increasingly lethargic
otherFindings: Difficult airway anticipated — swelling obscuring normal landmarks
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Barely audible whisper, unable to speak in full words

expectedActions.shortAction: Repeat epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (adult fixed dose, q5–15 min for persistent anaphylaxis)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If signs of anaphylaxis and hypoperfusion persist following the first dose of epinephrine, additional IM epinephrine can be repeated q5–15 minutes at above noted doses
expectedActions.rationale: Ongoing anaphylaxis with airway compromise requires repeat dosing rather than watching and waiting.

expectedActions.shortAction: Attempt SGA/advanced airway; escalate to surgical airway if unable to oxygenate/ventilate
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: When patients cannot be oxygenated/ventilated effectively using the above interventions, or when conventional airway approaches are impossible, surgical airway management is a reasonable option if the clinician has competency in the procedure and risk of death for not escalating airway management seems to outweigh the risk of a procedural complication
expectedActions.rationale: Near-complete obstruction from angioedema may not be resolvable with standard intubation, requiring escalation to a surgical airway.
